lead: On the last day of the civil year, the four readings work like an examination of conscience. Leviticus says that a wrong done to a neighbour must be repaired. Wisdom shows how quickly everything passes, except the reward of the righteous. First Timothy teaches contentment and sets our eyes on eternal life. Luke’s fig tree gives the whole day its tone: “let it alone for one more year”. The new year is mercy, and it is meant to bear fruit.

set: Leviticus 1–7 sets out the sacrifices. This passage closes the section on the guilt offering (5:14–6:7). In the Hebrew Bible these verses are numbered 5:20–26. It treats sins against a neighbour in matters of property, where a false oath has been sworn in God’s name.
str: vv. 1–3: the wrongs: deception, robbery, fraud, keeping what was found, false oaths.
vv. 4–5: restitution in full, with one-fifth added.
vv. 6–7: then the ram; the priest makes atonement, and there is forgiveness.
kw: A breach of faith. The cheated person is a neighbour, yet the text calls it a trespass “against the Lord”. Wronging a neighbour is wronging God.
An offering of reparation. Isaiah 53:10 uses the same word of the Suffering Servant: “an offering for sin”.
vv: you shall repay the principal amount and shall add one-fifth to it. You shall pay it to its owner when you realize your guilt.

Restitution comes first, and the victim is repaid before anything is offered at the altar. Jesus says the same: “first be reconciled” (Matthew 5:24). Zacchaeus does far more than the law requires (Luke 19:8).
The priest shall make atonement on your behalf before the Lord, and you shall be forgiven for any of the things that one may do and incur guilt thereby.
The list of sins ends with a sure promise: there is a way back.
ch: The Catechism says that many sins wrong our neighbour and that simple justice requires us to repair the harm, returning stolen goods and restoring a good name, and that absolution does not remove this duty (CCC 1459, 2412). Under the New Covenant, the one offering of Christ brings the forgiveness the old sacrifices pointed to (Hebrews 10:10–14).

set: The Book of Wisdom was written in Greek, most likely among the Jews of Alexandria in the first century BC. In this scene the ungodly, who had mocked the righteous, now see them vindicated (5:1–5) and speak with regret. Verses 7–10 are their words. Verses 14–16 give the author’s reply.
str: vv. 7–8: the regretful questions: what has arrogance profited us?
vv. 9–10: all has vanished, like a shadow or a ship’s track.
v. 14: the hope of the ungodly is like chaff and smoke.
kw: There and gone. Wealth and fame cast no lasting mark.
What the righteous have is not their own achievement stored up; it is “with the Lord”, kept by him.
vv: What has our arrogance profited us? And what good has our boasted wealth brought us?
Honest questions, but asked too late. The reader has the chance to ask them today.
like a ship that sails through the billowy water, and when it has passed no trace can be found,
A fine image for a year gone by. What remains is what was done in God.
But the righteous live forever, and their reward is with the Lord; the Most High takes care of them.
One of the clearest Old Testament words of hope beyond death, close to “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (3:1).
ch: The Catechism teaches that each person receives eternal retribution at death, in a particular judgment that refers the life to Christ (CCC 1021–1022). At the end of a year this passage is not meant to frighten. It helps us ask what lasts.

r.h: Fight the good fight of the faith
set: The letter is traditionally by Paul; some scholars think a later disciple wrote it. It is addressed to Timothy, left in charge at Ephesus (1:3). The author has just warned of teachers who treat godliness as “a means of gain” (6:5), and he answers by turning the phrase around: real gain is godliness with contentment.
str: vv. 6–8: enough is enough: food and clothing.
vv. 9–10: the trap of wanting to be rich.
vv. 11–12: the man of God: flee, pursue, fight, take hold.
kw: A word prized by the Stoics for self-sufficiency. For Paul it rests on God, not on oneself (see Philippians 4:11–13).
The text does not call money the root of evil. It says that the love of money is “a root of all kinds of evil”.
Athletic language, the struggle in the games. The present tense tells him to keep on with it.
vv: for we brought nothing into the world, so that we can take nothing out of it;
An old saying of the Bible (compare Job 1:21).
For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil,
Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life, to which you were called and for which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
The good confession may well be Timothy’s baptism, or his ordination. Every Christian may look back to a day on which a promise was made.
ch: The Catechism warns against greed and urges detachment from riches, which is needed for entry into the Kingdom (CCC 2536, 2544). A year’s accounts look different when a Christian reads them in this light.

set: Only Luke has this parable. Just before it, people have told Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate, and he has spoken of eighteen who died when a tower fell. He refuses to treat them as worse sinners, and says twice, “unless you repent, you will all perish” (13:3, 5). The parable answers the question: how long will God wait?

Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. Isaiah had sung of God looking for fruit in his vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7). Jesus speaks to his hearers, and through them to every reader: the point is each person’s response, not any people’s guilt.
str: v. 6: the owner comes looking for fruit.
v. 7: three years, nothing: “Cut it down!”
vv. 8–9: the gardener pleads for one more year, and promises to dig and manure.
¶ The story has no ending. We are not told what the tree does.
kw: Using up the soil without return. An empty life also takes up space that could bear fruit.
The same verb is used for “forgive” (compare Luke 23:34). The gardener’s plea is a word of mercy.
Hardly a noble word. The gardener is willing to get his hands dirty for the tree.
vv: So he said to the gardener, ‘See here! For three years I have come looking for fruit on this fig tree, and still I find none. Cut it down! Why should it be wasting the soil?’
Justice is real: fruit is expected.
He replied, ‘Sir, let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it.
Christian readers see Christ in the gardener, who stands between us and judgment and works on us. The extra year is not idle time; it is full of his labour.
If it bears fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’”
Mercy gives time, but time does not last forever.
ch: St Augustine preached on this parable, seeing in the manure the humble sorrow of the repentant sinner (in substance). God’s patience is “not wanting any to perish, but all to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9; CCC 1037). The Church reminds us of the urgency of conversion while there is time (CCC 1036).

qa: Is the parable a threat for the new year?

It is a warning wrapped in mercy. The owner’s word is true, and the gardener’s plea is stronger. A Christian ends the year not in fear, but in thanksgiving for the time given, and with the resolve to use it.
rite: Many Syro-Malabar parishes close the year with a service of thanksgiving. It is a good moment to do what the readings ask: to thank God for the year, to put right a wrong we have done, and to ask for the grace of one more year that bears fruit. The Holy Qurbana is the Church’s great thanksgiving.
study: Is there something I owe someone, in money or in good name, that I should put right before this year ends?
What fruit does the Lord look for in me in the year to come, and what “digging” may he have to do in me to bring it about?
